title: Word squares: tiny grids that read both ways
description: In a word square, the rows and columns spell the same words, like a crossword that mirrors itself. A three-by-three square is the perfect place to start.

body.heading: A grid with a mirror inside
paragraphs: Write these three words in a stack: BAT, ARE, TEN. Now read down the columns instead of across. The first column spells BAT, the second ARE and the third TEN — the grid reads the same in both directions. That is a word square.

Word squares are old. The most famous, the SATOR square, was carved in Roman times with five Latin words — SATOR, AREPO, TENET, OPERA, ROTAS — arranged so they read across, down, and even backwards. It has been found scratched into walls from Pompeii to England.

body.heading: Why squares are tricky
paragraphs: Every letter does double duty: it belongs to a row word and a column word at the same time. Choosing the first word fixes the first letter of every other word, so one greedy choice can paint you into a corner three rows later.

That is also why squares are such good training for crosswords and Scrabble. You learn to think about words by their skeletons — which letters they start with, and which letters they can offer to their neighbours.

body.heading: Try it: build a three-by-three
paragraphs: Start with the middle. In a three-letter square, a first word ending in a common letter, like T or E, gives the third row an easier start. If you get stuck, change the first word rather than forcing the last row.
Graduation challenge: a four-by-four square. CARD, AREA, REAR, DARK is a lovely one to check letter by letter — read the columns and confirm it works, then try to build a different one of your own.

takeaway: A word square is a crossword folded in half: every word you place must agree with itself in two directions.
